name: Lighting Plots and Cue Design
title: Lighting Plots and Cue Design
answer: Lighting plots and cue design are the documents and sequences that tell a lighting system what to do during a performance or virtual shoot. A plot shows fixture positions, types, channels, addresses, and power or data runs. Cue design maps those fixtures to looks, timings, and transitions across scenes. In theater and virtual set design, the same logic extends to LED volumes, projection, and real time rendering. This topic covers drafting, paperwork, console programming, and the visual language of light.

sections.body: Lighting plots and cue design are the documents and sequences that tell a lighting system what to do during a performance or virtual shoot. A plot shows fixture positions, types, channels, addresses, and power or data runs. Cue design maps those fixtures to looks, timings, and transitions across scenes. In theater and virtual set design, the same logic extends to LED volumes, projection, and real time rendering. This topic covers drafting, paperwork, console programming, and the visual language of light.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What it runs on: drafting software like Vectorworks Spotlight, console platforms like ETC Eos or grandMA3, and visualization tools like Capture or WYSIWYG. Data flows over DMX, Art-Net, sACN, and increasingly Ethernet based networks. Virtual sets add game engines, media servers, and camera tracking. AI tools may assist with previsualization, fixture layout suggestions, or cue timing, but they sit alongside, not replace, the control desk. The site tracks 732 AI tools, and only some touch this workflow.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: How the work is done: the designer reads the script or shot list, talks with the director and set designer, and decides where light should come from and how it should move. They draft the plot, assign channels and addresses, then build cue lists on the console. In virtual production, they also align practical fixtures with LED wall content and camera tracking so the light matches the rendered environment. Cue timing is rehearsed and refined, often with paper tech and dry tech before technical rehearsals. Documentation, magic sheets, and cue sheets keep the team synchronized.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance: lighting plots, cue stacks, and console show files are creative and technical records that may belong to the designer, the production, or the venue depending on contracts. Generated textures, gobos, projected media, and sound cues can raise copyright questions if their training data or source assets are unclear. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, which shows that provenance is an active concern across AI assisted media. Safety matters too, including electrical load, rigging limits, and eye safety with intense fixtures or lasers. Designers keep version histories and asset licenses so a cue can be traced and reproduced.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going: consoles and drafting tools are adding more automation, from fixture patch suggestions to cue timing based on audio or video analysis. Virtual production is pushing lighting plots closer to real time rendering, with LED volumes and camera tracking demanding tight synchronization. AI may help generate look variations, paperwork, and previsualization faster, but the designer still owns the artistic and safety decisions. Standards for data exchange and asset provenance will matter as more generated media enters the cue stack. The field is likely to blend traditional stage craft with virtual set workflows rather than replace one with the other.
